# Store setup checklist

## Purpose
Turn a setup or configuration task into an evidence-based pass/fail list instead of a settings-page glance, so nothing is marked done without being read.

## Steps
1. Pull the idea-bank items and required-state rules for the section in question.
2. Read the live configuration through the platform connector (Shopify Admin, WooCommerce REST API).
3. Compare live state to required state, one field or setting at a time.
4. For every fail, write down the exact evidence (the value read, the value required).
5. Write the fix, sized to whether a person or the founder needs to act.
6. Mark pass only where a live read confirmed it.

## Checks
- No item marked pass from memory or a settings screenshot alone.
- Every fail has a concrete, actionable fix.
- Evidence is dated so staleness is visible later.

## Output
A checklist table plus a one-line summary a founder can read in 10 seconds.

## Example
"Payment capture timing: FAIL. Live value: manual capture. Required: automatic within 3 days. Fix: change capture setting in Shopify Payments settings, 2 minutes, no dependency."

# Payments, shipping and tax setup

## Purpose
Configure the 3 setup areas where a wrong number costs real money on day one, and prove every one of them with a real test, not a settings screenshot.

## Steps
1. For payments: verify identity documents exactly, add a second gateway (Shop Pay, PayPal, Apple Pay, a BNPL option such as Affirm, Klarna or Afterpay) and regional methods, set capture and fraud rules.
2. Test every gateway in sandbox, then place and refund one real order before removing the storefront password.
3. For shipping: build zones so every country has an explicit rate, set the free-shipping threshold from real margin and AOV.
4. Test every rate bracket at its edge with a real cart.
5. For tax: confirm real obligations with a professional first, then enable the calculation service per jurisdiction (state nexus and marketplace facilitator rules for the US).
6. Decide inclusive/exclusive display and tax basis per jurisdiction's real rule, and test one product per tax class in 2+ regions.

## Checks
- A real refunded order exists in the gateway dashboard.
- Every shipping bracket boundary was tested with a real cart.
- No tax jurisdiction configured without a professional's sign-off on file.

## Output
One configuration + test log per area, each line naming the setting, the value, the test performed and the result.

## Example
"Free shipping threshold: set at $59, from AOV $46 and 42% margin. Tested at $58.99 (rate shown) and $59.00 (free), both correct."

# Pre-launch QA and launch sequencing

## Purpose
Prove, with real customer actions, that a store is actually ready to sell, and give one clear go or no-go call before the password comes off.

## Steps
1. Pull every prior setup workflow's result into one dependency-ordered list.
2. For each line, perform the real action a customer would take (browse, add to cart, pay, receive an email) rather than checking a setting.
3. Run a full mobile QA pass across the brand's real device split.
4. Check the logged-out storefront in an incognito window, clicking every visible element.
5. Compile the pass/fail table.
6. Give one clear go or no-go call, naming any blocking failure.
7. Remove the storefront password only once every line passes.

## Checks
- Every line closed with a real action, not an admin-panel glance.
- No password removal before 100% pass.
- The go/no-go call is unambiguous.

## Output
A pass/fail table plus a one-line go/no-go recommendation with any blocker named.

"38 of 38 checks pass. Go. Password removed 14:02 IST, confirmed by a live incognito purchase test immediately after."

## Purpose
Catch the small things quietly going wrong on a live store before they become a support flood or a lost sale, on a fixed weekly cadence.

1. Reconcile platform inventory against real stock (weekly for month one, then as risk warrants).

3. Re-run shipping and tax checks whenever a product, zone or app changed this week.

- Every recurring ticket cluster maps to a named root cause or is routed to the right specialist.

A short weekly hygiene report and a fix list, each fix naming who does it.

# Theme engineering practice

## Purpose
Pick a theme on real fit, not a demo, and keep every later change consistent with one documented set of design tokens instead of drifting section by section.

## Steps
1. Write the required feature and section list before opening any theme.
2. Vet each candidate on a real product page and a real mobile width, not the homepage demo.

4. Once a theme is live, document its color, spacing, typography and component tokens.
5. Check every new homepage or PDP section, native or page-builder, against the token set.

- Vetting happened on PDP and mobile, never the homepage demo alone.
- Every new section was checked against the token doc, not shipped by eye.

A scored theme shortlist for a selection task, or a token doc plus drift flags for an ongoing design-system check.

# AI build-agent guardrail

## Purpose
Keep an AI coding agent's storefront work safe and reviewable: real inputs, one change at a time, private preview, and manual QA before anything the agent wrote reaches a customer.

## Steps
1. Write a brief with the real product, policy and voice inputs the agent needs; never send it in with a bare one-line prompt.
2. Let the agent interview and propose a plan before it starts building.
3. Ask for exactly one storefront change per prompt, and verify each one live before the next.
4. Preview every change privately; never let the agent's output reach the public URL directly.
5. Treat the AI-authored section as a draft: run mobile QA and a claims check (shared/claim-check) on it.
6. Plan long sessions around a possible usage-limit pause so a half-finished change isn't left live.

## Checks
- Every AI-authored section passed a claim check before merge.
- No public URL ever served an unreviewed AI change.

## Output
The AI build brief used to start the session, a QA pass report, and a change log entry per shipped edit.

"Brief: rebuild the size-chart tab using the real size data in brand.json. Agent proposed a plan, built on a duplicate theme, previewed privately, claim-check passed, merged via reviewed PR."

# Git-based theme version control and CI

## Purpose
Replace duplicate-theme-in-admin editing with a real engineering workflow, so every change is reviewable by commit and reversible by command, not by remembering which duplicate is which.

## Steps
1. Connect the theme repo to GitHub and configure Shopify CLI for local development.
2. Add theme-check linting to run on every commit and block a merge on a hard error.
3. Stand up a staging theme URL that auto-deploys from a branch, mirroring production.
4. Require a second reviewer or the founder gate before any merge to the live theme.
5. Keep one tested command to redeploy the previous commit's theme package.
6. Tag each deploy with the change brief it shipped so the registry can trace it to an approved idea.
7. Refresh the staging store's product/price/inventory snapshot from production on a schedule, never the reverse.

## Checks
- Rollback has actually been exercised once, not just written down.
- Staging always mirrors current production data before a risky test.

## Output
A git repo with real commit history, working CI config, a live staging theme URL, and a rollback runbook.

## Example
"Deploy tagged to brief DEV-2026-091. Rollback tested: `shopify theme push --release=prev` restored the prior theme in 40 seconds."

# Platform, app and automation governance

## Purpose
Keep the store's app stack lean, its small operational rules automated without custom code, and its platform surface current, all under one governance discipline.

## Steps
1. Vet any candidate app against ratings and a real before/after speed test, never install on trust alone.
2. Consolidate apps doing the same job, and search for residual theme code after every uninstall.
3. List recurring manual if-this-then-that actions a store manager does by hand.
4. Wire each into the platform's native automation layer (Shopify Flow or equivalent), never a custom-coded rule for pure logic.
5. Test each rule against a real historical order before turning it on live, and log every action it fires.
6. Read each platform release (Shopify Editions, WooCommerce/WordPress core, app deprecations, API sunsets) on its own schedule.
7. Match new native features against the paid app list to flag a possible retirement, and write a short adopt-or-ignore memo.
8. For a brand with a mobile app, QA the store listing, screenshots, deep links and push opt-in before each release.

## Checks
- Every automation rule tested against a real order before going live, with its actions logged.
- No API key or credential appears anywhere outside the platform's own secure settings.

## Output
An app audit report, working automation rules with an audit log, a short per-release memo, and (when relevant) an app release QA report.

## Example
"Automation rule: auto-tag orders over $150 with a prior chargeback or return-to-sender history as 'high-risk-review'. Tested against 20 historical orders, correctly flagged 3 known cases, enabled live."

# Build a custom integration or webhook

## Purpose
Connect the store to an ERP, warehouse system, loyalty ledger, marketplace feed or courier safely, with retries and alerting instead of a silent, brittle one-way sync.

## Steps
1. Map every field that must sync both ways (inventory, order status, tracking number, loyalty points) before writing any code.
2. Build the custom app or Shopify Flow automation and register the needed webhooks.
3. Store API keys and tokens only in the platform's secure app settings or the environment secret store, never in theme code or a public repo.
4. Add retry-with-backoff on failed webhook deliveries, with a dead-letter log for ones that never succeed.
5. Alert a human the moment a sync gap is detected (order count mismatch, stale inventory timestamp).
6. Document the data contract so a future developer does not reverse-engineer it.
7. Test against a sandbox or staging account of the external system before pointing at production.

## Checks
- No credential appears outside the platform's secure settings.
- A deliberately failed test webhook triggers the retry logic and, if it keeps failing, a human alert.

## Output
A working integration or Flow, a retry log, a written data contract, and a sync-health alert rule.

## Example
"Inventory sync to the 3PL's WMS: field-mapped SKU, quantity, location. Retry with exponential backoff up to 5 attempts, dead-letter log after that, Slack alert to ops on any dead-letter entry."

# Automated regression and uptime monitoring

## Purpose
Catch a breaking theme/app change before it ships, and catch a live outage or slow degradation within minutes instead of at the next scheduled hygiene sweep.

## Steps
1. Map the store's critical paths (home, PDP, filter, cart, discount code, checkout, login) into test cases.
2. Run visual diffs across breakpoints and scripted end-to-end flows before and after every deploy, plus nightly.
3. Self-heal a test whose selector changed for a cosmetic reason; flag the ones that fail for a real reason.
4. On failure, capture video replay, console errors and a network trace, and write an actionable bug report.
5. Run synthetic checks every few minutes on home, PDP, cart, checkout and search from more than one region.
6. Run a full transaction walk (add-to-cart through confirmation) on a schedule, not just a page-200 check.
7. Track SSL and DNS separately, and pull real-user page-load data to catch slow-but-not-down degradation.
8. Route any failure or degradation to a human with an escalation path if unacknowledged, logging detect and fix time.

## Checks
- No deploy ships without a green regression run.
- Every incident logs a real detect time and fix time.

## Output
A pass/fail regression report with visual diffs and bug replays, plus an uptime dashboard and incident log.

## Example
"Nightly regression: checkout flow failed on Safari mobile after a tag-manager update. Video replay + network trace attached. Deploy blocked until fixed."

# Speed measurement, baseline and monitoring

## Purpose
Measure real page speed honestly, fix the page paid traffic actually lands on first, and keep a running budget so nothing regresses silently.

## Steps
1. Record every response of the real page with speed_lab.record before changing anything.
2. Measure 3 runs on a throttled mobile profile (Pixel 5, slow 4G, 4x CPU) and take the median.
3. Cross-check a suspicious lab result against PageSpeed Insights field data.
4. Fix the page paid ads land on before any other template.
5. Turn every diagnosed fix into a brief: what, needs, tradeoff, who, a numeric pass threshold, and a one-step rollback.
6. Re-audit monthly holding a page-weight and script-count budget, flagging the moment a budget is crossed.
7. Wait about 28 days of field data before calling a fix a win.
8. Before a known sale, list at-risk dynamic steps, load-test them, and freeze risky changes during the window.

## Checks
- Every measurement is 3 runs averaged, never 1.
- Field and lab data are read as separate things, never conflated.
- Every brief's threshold is a number, never a feeling.

## Output
A baseline measurement file, a diagnosis, a developer brief per fix, a monthly trend report, and (seasonally) a peak-readiness report.

# Cut image, font and code weight

## Purpose
Cut the 3 biggest sources of unnecessary page weight, in the right order, each proven with a before/after byte count.

## Steps
1. Check images directly; never trust automatic platform compression alone.
2. Resize to about 2,000px, use JPEG for photos and PNG only for transparency, confirm WebP/AVIF delivery, and set lazy-load below the fold, eager above it.

- Before/after byte counts recorded for every fix.

An image fix list, a font fix list, and a code-splitting plan, each with a before/after number.

Check that a page works for a real person: no dead controls, no hidden content on mobile, and no barrier for someone using a keyboard or a screen reader.

## Steps
1. Strip navigation to logo, cart and one CTA on single-offer campaign pages; open a cart drawer on add-to-cart, never a reload.
2. Fire pop-ups only on real intent signals, never in the first 3-5 seconds; fix or remove dead controls and false affordances.
3. Build and review every page mobile-first, on the brand's own real device split, checking every screen width in responsive mode.
4. Pin the PDP CTA on mobile without covering the variant selector; never hide reviews or content behind a mobile-only carousel; cap mobile forms at 4 fields.
5. Run an automated WCAG scan on home, PDP, collection, cart and checkout templates.
6. Manually test forms, navigation and dynamic states with a keyboard and a screen reader, separating real failures from automated false positives.
7. Scope every remediation to the theme codebase so fixes survive future updates.

## Checks
- Every friction fix confirmed live, not assumed from a screenshot.
- Mobile QA run on the brand's real device split, not a generic phone size.
- Manual accessibility pass included, not the automated scan alone.

## Output
A friction fix list, a mobile QA report with screenshots per width, and an accessibility audit report.

## Example
"Cookie banner covers the Add to Cart button on iPhone 13 at 390px width. Fixed by repositioning the banner; confirmed with a real screenshot at that exact width."

# Design the statistics of a CRO test

## Purpose
Size and design a test so its result can actually be trusted, since a wrong sample-size formula is a silent, expensive mistake.

## Steps
1. Decide test-or-not from the traffic gate and real sample-size math; below the threshold, recommend a bigger change instead.
2. Size the test from the minimum detectable effect, stated as orders per variant, never a flat number pulled from habit.
3. Compute runtime as arms x sample / weekly traffic, running at least 2 full weeks and covering each weekday twice.
4. Pick a stopping rule before launch and commit to it; no peeking outside the planned looks.
5. Randomize by user with sticky bucketing so a visitor never sees both arms.
6. Remove or isolate returning-visitor traffic so it doesn't contaminate a new-visitor test.

## Checks
- Sample size is orders per variant, computed from a real MDE, not a round number.
- Stopping rule exists in writing before the test goes live.

## Output
A test design spec: arms, sample size, runtime, stats engine, stopping rule, randomization method.

## Example
"MDE: 8% relative lift on PDP-to-cart. Required: 2,400 orders per variant. At current 850 orders/week split across 2 arms, runtime: 3 weeks. Stopping rule: fixed horizon, no early peek."

# Read and interpret CRO test results

## Purpose
Turn raw test numbers into an honest verdict, catching the common ways a test result lies: bad luck days, sample mismatch, novelty, and p-value tunnel vision.

## Steps
1. Count conversions on a real confirmation event (a purchase), never a click proxy.
2. Never call a test on the strength of one especially good or bad day.
3. Check sample ratio mismatch at launch and at every planned look.
4. Plot novelty and primacy effects daily before trusting the average.
5. Check the mobile-only and desktop-only splits separately before shipping a win.
6. Apply Twyman's law: audit any surprising win harder than an expected one before celebrating it.
7. Decide from the confidence interval and the real business value together, never p<0.05 alone.
8. Treat a fully powered inconclusive test as a real, useful result, not a failure to hide.

## Checks
- No verdict rests on a p-value alone.
- SRM, novelty and device splits are all checked before a result is trusted.

## Output
A result read report and a clear ship/hold/kill recommendation.

## Example
"Variant B: +11% PDP-to-cart, CI [3%, 19%], SRM clean, no novelty decay by week 2, consistent on mobile and desktop. Recommendation: ship."

# Roll out winners and protect them over time

## Purpose
Ship a winner properly and prove it stays a winner, since a shipped test can silently regress or get overwritten by a later, unrelated change.

## Steps
1. Ship the winner as the new control for the next challenger test.
2. Re-audit the page after the change ships.
3. Re-verify with fresh session recordings, funnel rate and a re-survey once real post-ship data exists.
4. Run an LTV and returns check before scaling any angle- or claim-driven win, since a short-term lift can mask a long-term return problem.
5. Keep a live-winner register of every shipped test.
6. Re-check quarterly that every past winner is still live and unbroken by a later change.
7. Set founder expectations at a 10-20% win rate for PDP/cart/checkout tests, so a string of inconclusive tests doesn't read as failure.

## Checks
- Re-verification happens after shipping, not assumed from the pre-ship test result.
- Every past winner is re-checked live at least once a quarter.

## Output
A winner register entry per shipped test, and a quarterly protection check report.

## Example
"Q3 protection check: 6 of 7 shipped winners still live and measuring as expected. 1 (free-shipping bar) was overwritten by an unrelated theme update in August; restored and re-verified."

# Design holdout and incrementality measurement

## Purpose
Prove a feature or a whole programme is adding real value with a holdout, since a feature's own engagement metric and the sum of individual test lifts both overstate value.

## Steps
1. Design a feature holdout (a popup, a recommendation module, a cart-recovery flow) instead of trusting its own engagement metric.
2. Run a persistent programme-level holdout to prove the CRO programme's net value, never reported as the sum of test lifts.
3. State the identifying assumption behind any causal method in writing, and actively try to challenge it.
4. Check the traffic gate before choosing a holdout design; a traffic-starved brand may not support a clean holdout.
5. Turn on CUPED variance reduction only for returning, identified users.
6. Winsorize outlier orders or switch to a proportion metric to steady a noisy revenue test.

## Checks
- Programme value is never reported as the sum of individual test lifts.
- The identifying assumption is written down, not left implicit.

## Output
A holdout design and a programme value report.

## Example
"Cart-recovery discount flow: holdout group with no discount converts at 62% of the discounted group's recovery rate; net incremental revenue after the discount cost is still positive but smaller than the raw recovery-rate lift suggested."

Make sure a PDP's price-comparison claim never goes stale or false, by watching the same public competitor prices already used as signal elsewhere, without ever copying competitor text, images or branding.

## Steps
1. Read only publicly listed competitor prices already treated as signal elsewhere in the system, never scraped account data.
2. Match each PDP anchor-price or comparison claim to the specific competitor price it cites.
3. Flag a claim as stale the moment the cited price changes enough to make the comparison inaccurate.
4. Propose the corrected comparison number for a human to approve before any copy changes.
5. Never let a comparison claim ship without a current, dated source behind it.
6. Keep this entirely separate from the brand's own private cost and margin data.

## Checks
- Every live comparison claim has a current, dated public source.
- No comparison copy ever changes without a human approving the correction first.

## Output
Stale-claim flags and proposed corrected comparison copy, both handed to a human for approval.

## Example
"PDP claims 'save ₹500 vs [competitor]'s listed price of ₹2,499'. Competitor now lists at ₹2,199. Flagged stale; proposed correction: 'save ₹200', pending founder approval."

# Run holiday and gifting operations

## Purpose
Turn a store into gift-buying mode on schedule, without ever promising a delivery date the carrier can't keep, and turn it back off cleanly afterward.

## Steps
1. Confirm the gifting window and its cutoff dates from the shared gifting calendar 60 days out.
2. Turn on gift wrap and a gift-message option on relevant products.
3. Build a price-hidden gift invoice path so a recipient never sees the price paid.
4. Set delivery-by-date cutoffs per ZIP code from real carrier data (per pincode where the brand sells in India), never a flat national promise.
5. Build gift guides grouping the catalogue by recipient and occasion, using only real product and price data.
6. Switch relevant PDPs and the homepage to gifting-mode messaging for the window's duration.
7. QA the full gift-wrap-to-hidden-price-to-delivery-cutoff path as a real gift buyer would experience it.
8. Switch everything back to normal mode the day after the window closes, and log cutoff accuracy for next year.

## Checks
- No gift order ever promises a delivery date the ZIP code's (or pincode's) real cutoff cannot support.
- Gifting mode is confirmed fully reverted after the window.

## Output
Gift wrap/message configuration, a hidden-price invoice flow, a ZIP code delivery cutoff map (pincode map for India), and gift guide pages.

## Example
"Black Friday and Cyber Monday window: cutoff set at 3 business days before December 25 for standard shipping zones, 6 days for remote ZIP codes, pulled from real carrier transit-time data, not a single national date. India market option: Diwali window cutoff set at 3 days before the festival for metro pincodes, 6 days for others."

# Route an out-of-scope finding to the owning specialist

## Purpose
Hand off a finding that belongs to another specialist, with the evidence, instead of quietly dropping it or executing it outside Site's real expertise.

## Steps
1. Name the right owning specialist: Lifecycle (welcome/cart-recovery/win-back automation, VIP segmentation), Organic (organic social cadence, technical SEO), Product (pre-build demand validation), Brand strategist (a full repositioning call), or Money and ops (broader measurement/P&L tracking).
2. Package the observed condition and its evidence, not a finished brief the other specialist didn't ask for.
3. State plainly why this is not Site's job, in one sentence.
4. File the note to the registry so the owning specialist can pick it up on their own schedule.

## Checks
- The note names a specific owning specialist, not a vague "someone should look at this".
- Evidence is attached, not just an assertion.

## Output
One short handoff note per finding: {finding, evidence, which specialist, why it is theirs not Site's}.

## Example
"Finding: no cart-recovery email sends after checkout abandonment (30 days of Shopify data show 0 sends). Evidence: attached export. Routes to: Lifecycle. Why: automated recovery messaging is Lifecycle's folder, not Site's."
